task: I got a rejection email for a marketing coordinator role today. Write a reply thanking them, saying I'm still interested in future openings, and asking if they'd be willing to share one or two points of feedback on my application.
rewrite:
ambition:     Keep it short (under about 120 words) and make the feedback ask easy to say yes to. A strong recruiter-savvy candidate would thank the sender by name, mention one specific thing from the process, and ask a narrow question: "one or two points," answerable in a quick reply, with no call required.

agency:       The raw material is the rejection email itself: the sender's name, the exact role title, how far the process went, and any reason already given. It isn't pasted here, so assume a generic process and leave blanks for the sender's name and the person's own name. Pasting the rejection email would let the reply reference what was actually said.

acceleration: Reply in the same email thread so the role and context stay attached. Use the standard gracious-decline structure: thanks, then continued interest, then a specific ask, then an easy close. A LinkedIn connection request to the sender afterward keeps the contact warm.

accuracy:     Nothing outside the model can confirm this works until the sender replies. The closest proxy is checking the draft against the actual rejection email (name, title, stage reached) and having someone unfamiliar read it cold to see whether the ask is clear in ten seconds.

deeper task:
Write a reply to a rejection email for a marketing coordinator role. It should be brief, warm, and professional, in the voice of a candidate who wants to stay on the company's radar. Open by thanking the sender by name for their time and for considering the application. Say the person remains interested in future openings, especially in marketing. Then ask whether they'd be willing to share one or two points of feedback on the application, making clear a short reply is plenty and there's no need for a call. Close graciously. Use [Recruiter name] and [Your name] as the only blanks, with a subject line suited to replying in the existing thread. Keep the tone sincere and free of pleading, defensiveness, or filler, and keep it under about 120 words.

answers.plain:
**Subject:** Re: Marketing Coordinator Application

Hi [Name],

Thank you for letting me know, and for taking the time to consider my application for the Marketing Coordinator role. I enjoyed learning more about [Company] and the team.

I'm still very interested in working with [Company], and I'd love to be considered for future openings that fit my background.

If you're willing, I'd really appreciate one or two points of feedback on my application or interview. Any insight into how I could strengthen my candidacy would be very helpful as I continue my search.

Thank you again for your time and consideration.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

---

If you didn't interview, you can drop "or interview" and the line about learning more about the company. If you'd like, I can make it shorter or more formal.
answers.nudge:
**Subject:** Re: Marketing Coordinator Application – Thank You

Hi [Recruiter/Hiring Manager's name],

Thank you for letting me know, and for the time you and the team spent reviewing my application and speaking with me [include if you interviewed: "especially the conversation with you and [interviewer name] about [specific topic]"].

I enjoyed learning more about [Company]'s approach to [specific detail, e.g., the recent product launch, brand voice, or community campaigns]. I'm still very interested in the company and would love to be considered for future openings on the marketing team.

If you have a moment, I'd be grateful for one or two points of feedback on my application, such as areas where I could strengthen my experience or how I presented it. I'm working on growing as a marketer, and even a sentence or two would help.

Thanks again for your consideration. I hope our paths cross again.

Best regards,
[Your name]
[LinkedIn URL or portfolio link]
[Phone number]

---

**Tips to make it work harder for you**

- **Personalize the bracketed parts.** One specific detail about the company or interview shows real interest and makes you memorable. Without it, this reads as a template.
- **Send it within 24 to 48 hours.** Responding promptly and graciously leaves a good impression.
- **Keep the feedback ask small.** "One or two points" is easy to answer. Many companies won't reply for legal or policy reasons, so don't take silence personally.
- **If they do reply, thank them briefly and don't push back.** Arguing with or asking follow-up questions about the feedback can undo the goodwill.
- **Connect on LinkedIn** with the recruiter or hiring manager, with a short note like "Thanks again for the opportunity, I'd love to stay in touch." Then set up a job alert for the company's careers page.

**Shorter version, if you didn't get far in the process:**

> Hi [Name],
>
> Thank you for the update and for considering my application for the Marketing Coordinator role. I'm still very interested in [Company] and would welcome the chance to be considered for future openings.
>
> If you're able to share one or two points of feedback on my application, I'd really appreciate it and would use it to improve.
>
> Thanks again,
> [Your name]

If you tell me the company, whether you interviewed, and what you liked about the role, I can tailor the draft further.
